speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although some important federal government data have been delayed due to the shutdown, the public- and private-sector data that have remained available suggest that the outlook for employment and inflation has not changed much since our meeting in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Conditions in the labor market appear to be gradually cooling, and inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, and in light of the balance of risks to employment and inflation, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to lower our policy interest rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also decided to conclude the reduction of our aggregate securities holdings as of December 1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Available indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a moderate pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at a 1.6 percent pace in the first half of the year, down from 2.4 percent last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Data available prior to the shutdown show that growth in economic activity may be on a somewhat firmer trajectory than expected, primarily reflecting stronger consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Business investment in equipment and intangibles has continued to expand, while activity in the housing sector remains weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The shutdown of the federal government will weigh on economic activity while it persists, but these effects should reverse after the shutdown ends.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, the unemployment rate remained relatively low through August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job gains have slowed significantly since earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing likely reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and labor force participation, though labor demand has clearly softened as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although official employment data for September are delayed, available evidence suggests that both layoffs and hiring remain low, and that both households’ perceptions of job availability and firms’ perceptions of hiring difficulty continue to decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this less dynamic and somewhat softer labor market, the downside risks to employment appear to have risen in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index suggest that total PCE prices rose 2.8 percent over the 12 months ending in September and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These readings are higher than earlier in the year, as inflation for goods has picked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, disinflation appears to be continuing for services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up, on balance, over the course of this year on news about tariffs, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point to 3¾ to 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Higher tariffs are pushing up prices in some categories of goods, resulting in higher overall inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A reasonable base case is that the effects on inflation will be relatively short lived—a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent, and that is a risk to be assessed and managed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to ensure that a one-time increase in the price level does not become an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the near term, risks to inflation are tilted to the upside and risks to employment to the downside—a challenging situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There is no risk-free path for policy as we navigate this tension between our employment and inflation goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our framework calls for us to take a balanced approach in promoting both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With downside risks to employment having increased in recent months, the balance of risks has shifted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Accordingly, we judged it appropriate at this meeting to take another step toward a more neutral policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With today’s decision, we remain well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We continue to face two-sided risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the Committee’s discussions at this meeting, there were strongly differing views about how to proceed in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A further reduction in the policy rate at the December meeting is not a foregone conclusion—far from it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is not on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee also decided to conclude the reduction of our aggregate securities holdings as of December 1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our long-stated plan has been to stop balance sheet runoff when reserves are somewhat above the level we judge consistent with ample reserve conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Signs have clearly emerged that we have reached that standard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In money markets, repo rates have moved up relative to our administered rates, and we have seen more notable pressures on selected dates along with more use of our standing repo facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, the effective federal funds rate has begun to move up relative to the rate of interest on reserve balances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These developments are what we expected to see as the size of our balance sheet declined and warrant today’s decision to cease runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the three and a half years that we have been shrinking our balance sheet, our securities holdings have declined by $2.2 trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As a share of nominal GDP, our balance sheet has fallen from 35 percent to about 21 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In December, we will enter the next phase of our normalization plans by holding the size of our balance sheet steady for a time while reserve balances continue to move gradually lower as other nonreserve liabilities such as currency keep growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to allow agency securities to run off our balance sheet and will reinvest the proceeds from those securities in Treasury bills, furthering progress toward a portfolio consisting primarily of Treasury securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This reinvestment strategy will also help move the weighted average maturity of our portfolio closer to that of the outstanding stock of Treasury securities, thus furthering the normalization of the composition of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos, the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, are you uncomfortable with how market pricing has assumed a rate cut is a foregone conclusion at your next meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, as I just mentioned, a further reduction to the policy rate at the December meeting is not a foregone conclusion, as I’ve just said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say that that needs to be taken on board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had—you know, I would just say this—19 participants on the Committee, everyone works very hard at this and takes their obligations to serve the American people very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And at a time when we have tension between our two goals, we have strong views across the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I mentioned, they were strongly differing views today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the “takeaway” from that is that we haven’t made a decision about December, and we’re going to be looking at the data that we have, how that affects the outlook and the balance of risks, and I’ll just say that.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: You and some of your colleagues have framed last month and maybe today—I won’t put words in your mouth—as a risk-management exercise.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: At what point do you conclude that you’ve taken out enough insurance?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Are you looking for some kind of improvement in the outlook?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Or could this unfold along the lines of last year, where you made a sequence of adjustments and waited to gather more information?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the way we have been thinking—the way I’ve been thinking about it is the risks to the two goals—for a very long time, the risk was clearly of higher inflation, and then that has changed now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as we saw the—particularly after we saw—after the July meeting, we saw downward revisions in job creation, we saw a very different picture of the labor market and suggested that there were higher downside risks to the labor market than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that suggested that policy, which we had been holding at a, I would say, “modestly”—other people would say “moderately”—restrictive level, needed to move more in the direction, over time, of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the two goals are sort of equally at risk, then you ought to be at neutral, because one of them is calling for you to hike, and one of them is calling for you to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if that got back into balance, then you’d want to be roughly at neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So in that sense, it was a [case of] risk management, and I would say the same about today—sort of the same logic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as I mentioned, going forward is a different thing.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you for taking this question.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: We’ve just heard from you that the discussion in December and the conclusion that the discussion is not a foregone conclusion.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: I’d like to just dig into that a little bit more, about what sort of arguments were brought up.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Was there any consideration, for instance, of the investment we’re seeing in AI and some of the generation of household wealth through rises in stock prices related to the AI boom?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that’s a—that’s a factor in everyone’s assessment of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say it’s a driving factor, I don’t think, for anybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess I would say it this way: Once again, I would just point out that we have the situation where the risks are to the upside for inflation and to the downside for employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have one tool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It can’t do both of those—you can’t address both of those at once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got a very different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you have some people—people have different forecasts, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they’ll feel—they’ll forecast faster or slower progress on one or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they also have different levels of risk aversion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people—some will be more averse to inflation overruns, and some will be more averse to underruns of employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you put that together, and as you can see from the SEP and from the public discussion that goes on between the meetings when participants go out and talk, they’re very disparate views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they were reflected in strongly differing views in today’s meeting, as I pointed out in my remarks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what leads me to say that, that we haven’t made a decision about December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I always say that it’s a fact that we don’t make decisions in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But this is—I’m saying something in addition here, that it’s not—it’s not to be seen as a foregone conclusion—in fact, far from it.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Can I just ask you a quick follow-up on QT?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: How much of the fund impressions we’ve seen in money markets are related to the U.S. Treasury issuing more short-term debt?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That could be one of the factors, but the reality is that we’ve seen—the things that we’ve seen, higher repo rates and the federal funds rate moving up, these are the very things that we—that we look for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We actually have a framework for looking at the place we’re trying to reach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we said for a long time now is that when we feel like we’re a little bit or a bit above what we consider a level that’s ample that we would freeze the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, reserves will continue to decline from that point forward as nonreserve liabilities grow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this happened, some of it—some things have been happening for some time now, showing a gradual tightening in money market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, in the last, call it, three weeks or so, you’ve seen more significant tightening and I think a clear assessment that we’re at that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other thing is, we’re—the balance sheet is shrinking at a very, very slow pace now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve reduced it by half twice, and so there’s not a lot of benefit to be—to be holding on for it to get the last few dollars, because, again, when the balance sheet—reserves are going to continue to shrink as nonreserves grow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there was support on the Committee, as we thought about it, to go ahead with this and announce effective December 1 that we will be freezing the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the December 1 date gives the markets a little bit of time to adapt.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: So much of the rationale for cutting interest rates, even as inflation moves away from the 2 percent target, seems to be that there are these mounting downside risks to the labor market.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But if those don’t materialize and the labor market either stabilizes around current employment levels or even starts to strengthen somewhat, how would that change your perception of how much interest rates need to fall from here?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Would you then be a bit more concerned about underlying inflation and the possibility of second-round effects from tariffs?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I mean in principle if you were to see data that suggested that the labor market is strengthening or even that it’s stabilizing, that would certainly play into our decisions going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and we do have—we get some data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is a place where we get—for example, we get the state-level data on initial claims, which are sending sort of a signal of more of the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also get job openings, and we’ll get lots of survey data, we’ll get the Beige Book and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll have a—we’ll have a picture of what’s going on in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the fact that we’re not seeing an uptick in claims or a downtick, really, in openings suggests that you’re seeing maybe continued very gradual cooling, but nothing more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that does give you some comfort.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But if this shutdown lasts a while longer and you don’t have that data in hand, I’m just wondering how that hinders the Committee’s ability to assess the state of the labor market and make the right policy decisions.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And, also, how much is that factoring into the debate about December?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll—we get—I mentioned what we get in the labor area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We get some data in inflation, some data in economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll get—we’ll have a picture of what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also will have the Beige Book again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say we’re not going to be able to have the detailed feel of things, but I think if there were significant or material change in the economy one way or another, I think we’d pick that up through this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So in terms of how it might affect December, it’s really hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: December is a—the meeting’s, like, six weeks away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know what we’re going to get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If there is a very high level of uncertainty, then that could be an argument in favor of caution about moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ll have to see how it unfolds.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Steve Liesman, CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Mr. Chairman, can you characterize the meeting in terms of, you said, strongly differing views?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Was this a close call, this cut?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Or was it a close call maybe the other way, because you had dissents on both sides?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I was referring to the discussion about—to the extent it related to December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw we had two dissents, one for 50 and one for no cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was a strong, solid vote in favor of this cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The strongly differing views were really about the future, what does that look like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think people are saying—they’re noticing stronger economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Forecasters generally, broadly, have raised their economic growth forecast for this year and next year, in some cases quite materially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the meantime, we see a labor market that’s kind of—I don’t want to say “stable,” but it’s not clearly in motion, it’s not clearly declining quickly in any case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be just continuing to gradually cool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, people have different—they have different forecasts and expectations about the economy and different risk tolerances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there’s—you read the SEP, you read the speeches, you know there are differing views on the Committee and to the point where I said what I said.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Just a follow-up on the balance sheet.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: If you stop it—the runoff—now, does that mean you have to go back to actually adding assets sometime next year so that the balance sheet doesn’t shrink as a percent of GDP and become a tightening factor?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The place we’ll be on December 1 is that the size of the balance sheet is frozen, and as mortgage-backed securities mature, we’ll reinvest those in Treasury bills, which will foster both a more Treasury balance sheet and also a shorter duration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—in the meantime, if you freeze the size of the balance sheet, the nonreserve liabilities—currency, for example—they’re going to continue to grow organically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, because the size of the balance sheet is frozen, you have further shrinkage in reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And reserves is the thing that we’re—that we’re managing that has to be ample.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’ll happen for a time, but not a tremendously long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know exactly how long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at a certain point, you’ll want to start—you’ll want to start reserves to start gradually growing to keep up with the size of the banking system and the size of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll be adding reserves at a certain point, and that’s the last point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Even then we’ll be—we didn’t make decisions about this today, but we did talk today about the composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there’s a desire that the balance sheet be—right now it’s got a lot more duration than the outstanding universe of Treasury securities, and we want to move to a place where we’re closer to that duration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t made a decision about the ultimate endpoint, but we all agree that we want to move more in the direction of a balance sheet that more closely reflects the outstanding Treasuries, and that means a shorter-duration balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, this is something that’s going to be—take a long time and move very, very gradually, and I don’t think you’ll notice it in market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s the direction of things.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jonnelle.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: Jonnelle Marte with Bloomberg.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: How are officials interpreting the latest CPI report?

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: So some components came in lower than expected, but core inflation was still at 3 percent.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: So at this moment are—what are you learning about the drivers and, also, do you believe that the risks are greater that the Fed makes a mistake on employment or inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, okay, so the September CPI report, we didn’t get PPI after that, which is—which is important for translation into what we look at, which is PCE inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we can still make a pretty good assessment of what that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we get PPI, there might be some adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But so directionally, it was a little softer than expected, and we always break it down into the three components.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, basically, you’ve seen goods prices increasing, and that’s really due to tariffs, and that’s due—that’s compared to a longer-run trend of very, very mild deflation in goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s moving inflation up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the other side of that, good news—housing services inflation has been coming down and is expected to continue to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you remember, a year—a couple years ago, that’s the one that just, we kept expecting it to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now it’s doing—it’s been doing that for some time, and we expect to continue that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That leaves—the biggest category is services other than housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s kind of been moving sideways over the last few months, but a significant part of that is nonmarket services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t take a lot of signal about the tightness of the economy from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you add all that up, a couple of things to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One is that inflation away from tariffs is actually not so far from our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We estimate—people have different estimates of what that is, but it might be five- or six-tenths, and so if it’s 2.8, then core PCE, not including tariffs, might be 2.3 or 2.4, in that range, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not so far from your goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that—we look at that, and the thing about tariff inflation is the base case is that it will come, and it probably will increase further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is that it will be a one-time increase, and we’ve been very focused for all of this year at making sure that that’s the case and thinking carefully about what are the—what are the pathways through which it could become something else, troublesome inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One of those would be a really tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Another could be inflation expectations moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—we’re watching this very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s—it’s not the case that we’re just assuming that it’s going to be a one-time inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand fully that this is a risk we have to monitor and ultimately manage.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: With a stubborn services inflation, what are some of the things that the Fed could do to address that, and especially when we’re seeing potentially labor supply challenges?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, say that first— JONNELLE MARTE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Stubborn services inflation— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Oh, stubborn services inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, again, the part of services inflation that is—that isn’t coming down as we would like it to is the nonmarket part of nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, overall, that’s just something that we expect will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The nonhousing—the nonmarket part of it should come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It largely reflects higher stock prices and financial services that are imputed, rather than actually paid, is a big part of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But also, just—we think policy is still modestly restrictive in my telling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the kind of thing that should lead to a gradually cooling economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s one of the reasons you see a gradually cooling labor market, [it] is because Fed policy is modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that should also help get that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want to say, though, we’re absolutely committed to returning inflation to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at longer-term surveys or market pricing, you will see that that’s a credible commitment, and there should be no question that that’s where we’re going.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Great, thank you.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber, Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: So there’s a big investment boom in AI infrastructure right now, as you know, and wondering if the existence of such a boom would indicate that rates are not that restrictive after all, and could further rate cuts at this point perhaps fuel an excess level of investment there or market bubbles?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: How is the Fed thinking about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t—I don’t think that the—you’re right, there’s a—there’s a lot of data centers being built and other investments being made around the country and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And big U.S. companies are just investing a lot of resources in thinking about how AI, which will be based on those data centers, run through data centers, is going to affect their businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a big deal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think that the spending that happens to build data centers all over the country is especially interest sensitive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s based on longer-run, it’s—longer-run assessments that this is an area where there’s going to be a lot of investment and that’s going to drive higher productivity and that sort of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know how those investments will work out, but I don’t think they’re particularly interest sensitive compared to some of the other sectors.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: And then just a quick follow-up.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: You mentioned that you do have data that you’re looking at for inflation and growth in the absence of government data.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Could you give us a sense—and I think we know a lot about the jobs data that’s out there—can you give us a sense of what you’re looking at to track inflation in the absence of government data?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a lot of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it doesn’t replace government data, but you know all of these, it’s—I’ll just mention some of the many, many names: PriceStats, Adobe, and others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And for wage inflation, there’s ADP data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On spending—you’re going to ask about spending at some point—there are lots of other things that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s, again, it’s, it’s many, many different sources and, again, including what we get out of the Beige Book, which will be sort of—come out mid-cycle as always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it doesn’t replace the government data, but it gives us a picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I think if something material were happening, if there were material developments, I think we would pick that up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we’ll be able to have a very granular understanding of the economy while this—while this data is not available.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: I just wanted you to elaborate a little bit on what you said a moment ago about the lack—the continued shutdown making it more difficult to make a move in December, and that may make you more cautious.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: To the degree you are relying on private data that isn’t the gold standard or that you’re relying on your own surveys or the Beige Book, do you worry at some point you’re going to have to start making policy by anecdote?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is a temporary state of affairs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re going to do our jobs, we’re going to collect every scrap of data we can find, evaluate it, and think carefully about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s our jobs—that’s what we’re going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you ask me, “Could it affect the December meeting?”, I’m not saying it’s going to, but, yeah, you could imagine that—what do you do if—what do you do if you’re driving in the fog?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that could or could not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know how that’s going to play into things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may get—the data may come back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there’s a possibility that it would make sense to be more cautious about moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not— I’m not committing to that, I’m just saying it’s certainly a possibility that you would say, “We really can’t see, so let’s slow down.” HOWARD SCHNEIDER.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As a follow-up, in the debate on this meeting, we saw recently some pretty big layoff announcements coming from Amazon and others—wondering if that figured into the discussion at all that you’re starting to see the turn, this tension between growth and employment starting to be resolved to the detriment of employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, secondly, some of the stresses starting to appear in the bottom spur of the K, as they call it, household health premiums that are going to be—possibly be going up quite substantially, things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Has that started to become a factor in your policy discussion?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are—those are both things that we’re watching very, very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To start with the layoffs, you’re right—you see a significant number of companies either announcing that they are not going to be doing much hiring or actually doing layoffs, and much of the time they’re talking about AI and what it can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re watching that very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, yes, it could absolutely have implications for job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t really see it in the initial claims data yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, it’s not a surprise that we don’t—it takes some time for it to get in there—but we’re watching that really carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, again, don’t see it yet in the—in the initial claims data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the K-shaped economy thing, I would say the same thing, or similar thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are—if you listen to the earnings calls or the reports of big, public, consumer-facing companies, many, many of them are saying that there’s a bifurcated economy there and that consumers at the lower end are struggling and buying less and shifting to lower-cost products, but that at the top, people are spending at the higher income and wealth, and they’re—so much, much anecdotal data on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we think there’s something there—so.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So Mr. Chairman, I want to take another crack at the further reduction in rates is not a foregone conclusion in December—you said “far from it.” So if a cut might not be on the table for December because of lack of data, what is the other concerns then stem from?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So if it’s not lack of data as the reason December is not a foregone conclusion, what other things could be the concern then?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, perspectives of people on the Committee that we’ve now moved 150 basis points and that we’re down into—you’re into that range between 3 and 4, where most estimates of—many estimates of the neutral rate live in that 3 to 4 percent area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re there now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re above the median number for the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think there are people on the Committee who have higher estimates of the neutral rate, and that’s—you can argue these positions since it can’t be directly observed, the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think for some part of the Committee, it’s time to maybe take a step back and see whether there really are downside risks to the labor market, or see whether, in fact, the growth—that the stronger growth that we’re seeing is real.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ordinarily, the labor market is a better indicator of the momentum of the economy than the spending data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the allure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this case, that gives a more downbeat read.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people just have—again, we’ve cut 50 more basis points in the last two meetings and there was a sense, from some, “let’s pause here” kind of thing, and a sense from others wanting to go ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s why I say differing views—strongly differing views.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So on that division, then, you’re talking about going forward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So what’s more important in this division?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Is it inflation risks?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Is it employment risks?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Or is there a deeper philosophy division among the Board?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—look, everybody on the Committee is deeply committed to doing the right thing to achieve our goals: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You have differences on how to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as I mentioned, some of that is different forecasts, but a lot of it is also different risk aversions to the two different variables, which is common through, through all federal reserves, they’re—people just have different risk tolerances, let’s say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that leads you to people with disparate views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You will know that from the speeches you’ve been listening to from my colleagues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re at a place now where we have, in fact, cut two more times, and now we’re 150 basis points closer to neutral, wherever that may be, than we were a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there’s a growing chorus now of feeling like maybe this is where we should at least wait a cycle, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just what you think it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—and, again, you’ve seen it in the September Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve seen this in the public remarks of FOMC participants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now I’m telling you that’s what—that’s what you can expect in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m just telling you that’s what happened in the meeting.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Elizabeth.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Thank you so much.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Elizabeth Schulze with ABC News.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: What is your explanation for why the job market is weakening right now, and what will this rate cut do to improve the job market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the—I think there are two things affecting the job market, and one of them is just a dramatic reduction in the supply of new workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So and that’s two things— that’s declining labor force participation, which is a cyclical thing, and then there’s declining immigration—which is just a big policy change that actually began in the last Administration and has been accelerated now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a big part of the whole story is that supply-side story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, labor demand has declined, and so the labor—the unemployment rate has gone down, meaning that demand for workers has gone down a little more than supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what’s going on, and—but it is mostly a supply function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s mostly a function of the change in supply, I think and many people think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the question then is, what does—what does our tool do, which supports demand?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so—and I would just say, when you’re in a situation where job creation, if you adjust for likely overcounting in the way that BLS does its work, is pretty close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So maximum employment doesn’t, on a sustainable basis, doesn’t—if you’re making, creating zero jobs, if it’s in equilibrium, if it’s in balance, it’s a pretty, as I said before, pretty curious balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I thought, and many of my colleagues thought—in fact, you’ve seen the last two meetings that it was appropriate for us to react by supporting demand with our rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve done that—we’ve reduced so that rates are looser.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that they’re accommodative right now, but they’re meaningfully less tight than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that should help so that at least the labor market doesn’t get worse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a complicated situation, and some people argue that this is supply and we really can’t affect it much with our tools, but others argue, as I do, that there is an effect from demand, and that we should use our tools to support the labor market when we see this happening.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: You also talked about tariffs causing a one-time price increase.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Should American households, consumers expect that inflation will continue to go up this year because of those tariffs?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the basic expectation is that there will be some additional increased inflation because it takes a while for tariffs to work their way through the production chain and finally get to consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we see this now from the tariffs that were put in place now many months ago—we see those effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you put tariffs in effect—and they’ve been coming into effect consistently in February, March, April, May—and that’s all happening, so that’ll continue to happen for some time, probably into the spring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are not big increases, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are a tenth or so on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They may be big increases on a particular product that’s been tariffed, but, overall, these are fairly modest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think some projections—we’re at 2.8 percent inflation—you might get two or three more tenths, or four more tenths maybe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But then, as all the tariffs are in, they stop generating inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve had a one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As long as you’re not—at least this is the theory, this is how we believe and hope that it will work out—once the last tariff is put on something, at that point it becomes a higher price level, but it stops going up, if you will, prices stop going up, they’ll just be at that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then measured inflation will come back down to non-tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as I mentioned, non-tariff inflation is not so far from 2 percent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, consumers are not interested in that story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Their prices are higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: More than that, the reason they’re so unhappy about inflation is the inflation that we had in 2021, ’22, ’23—because you can say that prices aren’t going up as much, but that doesn’t mean people aren’t feeling those higher prices from the inflation we had two or three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, I think, a large part of why the public—you sample people, inflation is still very much making people quite unhappy, even—and it’s nice that prices are not going up as fast as they were, but they’re still much higher than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’ll take some time for that effect to wear off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As real incomes rise, it will feel better over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s going to take time.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mike.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Television and Radio.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Do you have any concerns that equity markets are—or are close to being—overvalued at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we don’t look at any one asset price and say, “Hey, that’s wrong.” It’s not our job to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at the overall financial system, and we ask whether it’s stable and whether it could withstand shocks, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So banks are well capitalized, while some households are clearly under stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the aggregate, households are in good shape financially—relatively, relatively manageable levels of debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the lower-income spectrum, you are seeing rising defaults, particularly in subprime auto, but, nonetheless, in the aggregate pretty good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you don’t see—so you don’t see too much leverage in the banking system or the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a mixed picture, but it’s not an overly troubling picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, I’m not—it’s not appropriate—we don’t set asset prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Markets do that.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Well, are you—you must be well aware by lowering interest rates you’re contributing to additional asset price increases.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: And I wonder how you balance the idea that lowering rates would help the labor market with the reality that it seems more likely to be stimulating increased investment in AI, which is the rationale for thousands of job cuts that have been announced in the last few weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I don’t—I don’t think interest rates are an important part of the AI—the data center story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—people think there are great economics in building these data centers, and they’re making a lot of money building them, and I think they have very high present value and all that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not really—it’s not about 25 basis points here or there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We use our tools to support the labor market and to create price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s our two jobs, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re here to—by lowering rates at the margin, that will support demand, and that will support more hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s why we do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, no 25 basis point or even 50 basis point hike is going to be a dispositive thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, lower rates will support more demand, and that’ll support hiring over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, we also have to be careful about this, which is what we’ve been doing because we know where inflation is and we know—I’ve told you the story, this complicated story, but this is the best assessment that we can make and—but because there’s uncertainty around inflation and the path ahead for inflation, that’s why we’re going—that’s why the pace we’re going has been a careful one.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida from Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: On AI, I’m just wondering, it seems like a lot of the economic growth that we’ve been seeing is fed by investments in AI.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So how worried are you about what the sudden contraction in tech investment would mean for the overall economy?

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Is there enough strength in other sectors?

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: And, specifically, are there any lessons that you take from the 1990s in how you might approach what’s happening right now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—this is different in the sense that these companies—the companies that are so highly valued—actually have earnings and stuff like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you go back to the ’90s and the dot-com [period], they were—these were ideas rather than companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—so there’s a clear bubble there, whereas the—I won’t go into particular names, but they actually have earnings, and it looks like they have business models and profits and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s really a different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the investment we’re getting in equipment and all those things that go into creating data centers and feeding the AI, it’s clearly one of the big sources of growth in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending also, though, has been—is much bigger than that and has been growing and has defied a lot of, you know, negative forecasts, continuing to do so this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumers are still spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, it is—it may be mostly higher-end consumers or maybe skewed that way, but the consumer spending—and that’s a big, big chunk of what’s going on in the economy, bigger than—substantially bigger than AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You could point to growth—I mean, actually, maybe—growth as opposed to level, but consumer spending is a much bigger part of the economy.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: And why do you think that the labor market is slowing so much, even though consumer spending is strong?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Why has it slowed so much?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, what’s happened is that the supply of workers has dropped very, very sharply due to mainly immigration, but also lower labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means there’s less need for new jobs, because there’s—there isn’t this flow into the pool of labor where people need jobs because there aren’t those people now, so there’s not a supply of workers showing up for jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, demand has also gone down and so has—labor force participation has declined, which is more of a sign, in this case, of demand as well as trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think you’re seeing some softening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is growing at a slower rate than it was—2.4 percent last year, we think around 1.6 percent this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It could have been a couple of tenths higher if not for the shutdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, that will reverse, but you’ve still got the economy growing at a moderate pace.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Hey there—Andrew Ackerman with the Washington Post.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I wanted to ask if you could elaborate on how you think about policy in the context of the data drought.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Does it make you inclined to stick with your plans as set out in September in the absence of the data that might change your mind, or does it make you inclined to proceed with added caution because of uncertainty?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, well, we’ll know when we face that question—if we face that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—it’ll probably be argued both ways, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’ve said a couple times here that if you—if you really aren’t getting information, you really don’t know, and the economy looks like it’s solid and stable and hasn’t really changed, there will be an argument, I don’t know how persuasive it will be, but there will be an argument that you slow down in a—when you can’t see as far ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Others may argue—I’m not sure where this argument will come, but you’re perfectly right that you could also argue, things haven’t really changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you might not know that, so I don’t know whether we’ll face this or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I hope we don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I hope by the time of the December meeting, we’re getting a better flow of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if we—we’re going to have to do our jobs one way or the other.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Okay.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I also just wanted to ask a FinReg question.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: I think several years ago, you said the overall amount of capital in the system was about right.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: As the Fed moves forward with a revised Basel proposal, potentially changes to the G-SIB surcharge, has that changed at all?

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Or are you planning to significantly reduce the amount of capital in the system?

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s discussions going on, I think, among the agencies, and I don’t want to get ahead of those discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I continue to think that the level of capital, when I said that in 2020, was about right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, there’s been much capital added since then, through various mechanisms, but I look forward to—I know these discussions are really just getting going, they haven’t come to the point where they’re—where they’ve got a whole plan and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I really don’t have much to say on that.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Brian.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Hi, Chairman Powell.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Brian Cheung with NBC News.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Is the weakness in the jobs market accelerating, and who’s at risk if the interest rate cuts are not the effective medicine for a further slowdown in the labor market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do not see the weakness, as you put it, the weakness in the job market accelerating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say, then again, we don’t have—we didn’t get the September employment report, payroll report, but we do get—we look at the unemployment insurance claims, initial claims are reported at the state level, and we still get those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we can cumulate them and get the national number, and there’s really—I mean, there’s no story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can look at the numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Same thing with the job openings we get from Indeed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s just no story over the last four weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s kind of stable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you don’t see anything that says that the job market—or, really, any part of the economy—is making a significant deterioration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see more things, like I mentioned, though, which is that you see big companies making announcements of either layoffs or of the idea that they can—they won’t need to hire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Their number of employees is not expected to go up over a number of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There may be different people working there then—they say that too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they don’t need a bigger head count.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you see those kinds of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t see it in the aggregate numbers—the layoff numbers have not gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But job creation is very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the job-finding rate for people who are unemployed is very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the unemployment rate is very low as well, 4.3 percent is a low employment—unemployment rate.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: And so, as you make these cuts, is it the lower-income workers that you’re thinking about, or those who might have their jobs automated?

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Is there a particular— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: That we’re thinking of?

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: —section of the labor market that you’re particularly— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: So, we can’t—our tools don’t allow us to target any demographic or any income level and that kind of thing.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: I do think that people—we saw this during the Global Financial Crisis and the long recovery.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: If you have a long period of very strong labor market conditions, it benefits people at the lower end the most.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: The last two or three years of that long expansion, people at the lower part of the income spectrum were getting the biggest benefits, and lots of things were happening in that space, demographically, which were very constructive.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: And we’re not at that place right now.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: But so, yeah, a stronger labor market is the best thing we can do for the public.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: It’s also part of our job.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: It is half of our job.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: But it is absolutely the best thing we can do for people, along with keeping prices stable.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Those two things.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: I mean, inflation also hurts people on fixed incomes more than other people.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Courtenay.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Courtenay Brown from Axios.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: As you know, the 12 Reserve Bank presidents’ terms are up for renewal at the end of February.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: I’m wondering if you can give us a timeline for when the Board will consider those reappointments and whether we can expect everyone to be re-upped or if we can expect some changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a process that we go through, under the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The way the law works is, we have a reappointment process every five years for all of the—all of the Reserve—each of them and all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re in the middle of that process, and we’re going to complete it in a timely way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I really—that’s really all I can say.

speaker: COURTENAY BROWN
sentence: Okay, thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Daniel.

speaker: DANIEL AVIS
sentence: Daniel Avis, Agence France-Presse.

speaker: DANIEL AVIS
sentence: You now have dissents in three consecutive FOMC meetings, but in this meeting you had dissents going in both directions.

speaker: DANIEL AVIS
sentence: And you just mentioned the strong disagreement over the future path of rate cuts.

speaker: DANIEL AVIS
sentence: Have these disagreements complicated your role presiding over the FOMC meetings?

speaker: DANIEL AVIS
sentence: And, if so, how?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that, no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you—you have to take what comes, and what comes right now is a pretty challenging situation where we have—first of all, we have 4.3 percent unemployment, we have an economy that’s growing close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, it’s a good picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a good picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in terms of our policy, we have upside risks to inflation, downside risks to employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is a very difficult thing for a central bank, because one of those calls for rates to be lower, one calls for rates to be higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can’t do both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have to balance the two, and so it’s a challenging thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as we have worked our way through this process, you would expect that there would be a range of views across the Committee on what to do and the speed with which we should do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That makes a lot of sense to me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are—all of these people are people who take their jobs very seriously, work very hard at this, and just want to do what’s right for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they have different views on what that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s an honor to work among people who care that much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I don’t feel that it’s unfair or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just—it’s a time when we’re making quite difficult judgments in real time, and I believe we’ll get through this, and I think we’ve done sort of the right things so far this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we were—it was appropriate for us to be careful about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it would not be appropriate to just ignore or assume away the inflation issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, I think the risk of higher, more persistent inflation has declined significantly since April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if we do wind up resuming rate cuts at some point—we will at some point—I think we’re trying to get to the end of this cycle with the labor market in a good place and with inflation on its way to 2 percent or at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s all we’re trying to do, and we’re doing it under quite challenging circumstances and doing the best we can.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: We’ll go to Jennifer, for the last question.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Thank you so much, Chair Powell.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Both regional and large banks have taken losses on loans given delinquencies on subprime auto loans.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: JPMorgan’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, warned when you see one cockroach, there may be more likely.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: I’m curious how the Fed is looking at these loan losses and if it poses risks to the financial system or the outlook for the economy.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Is it a warning sign?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we’re—obviously we watch these things very carefully, credit conditions very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re right—you’ve seen rising defaults in subprime credit for some time now, and now you’ve seen a number of subprime credit—automobile credit institutions having significant losses, and some of those losses are now showing up on the books of banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking at it carefully, we’re paying close attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see, at this point, a broader credit issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t seem to be something that has very broad application across financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re going to be—we’re going to be monitoring this quite carefully and making sure that that is the case.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: And then, separately, many—you yourself have said that we’re in a bifurcated economy right now with high-net-worth individuals continuing to spend, with the lower income pulling back.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: How much of consumer spending continuing hinges on the stock market remaining strong?

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: In some odd way, does the market help keep the economy buoyant?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there is some—there is some relationship there, but, remember, the more wealth someone has, the lower an additional dollar of wealth matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So your marginal propensity to consume declines quite dramatically as you reach—as you reach levels of stock market wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the stock market—it would affect spending if the stock market went down, but it wouldn’t drop—it wouldn’t drop sharply unless there were quite a sharp drop in the stock market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People at the lower end of income and wealth have a much higher marginal propensity to consume an incremental dollar of income or wealth, but they don’t have the stock market wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s certainly a factor supporting consumption right now, but—and you would see it if you saw material corrections in spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it wouldn’t be—you shouldn’t think that it’ll, dollar for dollar, stop consumption, because that wouldn’t be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
